name: British Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Sign language (BSL); prosody literature exists but no spoken-style word-stress description; not applicable to stress databases.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy. 2010. Prosody and syntax in sign languages. Transactions of the Philological Society 108(3): 298-328. doi:10.1111/j.1467-968x.2010.01242.x (PMC3250094 author manuscript).
sources.note: General sign-language prosody survey (ISL/ASL data). Reports phrase-final prominence in phonological and intonational phrases (Nespor & Sandler 1999 for ISL; Wilbur 1999 for ASL: 'prominence on the final sign of IPs'); fn. 5: 'Klima and Bellugi (1979) write that stress falls on the second member of a compound in ASL'; fn. 10: 'Little is said here about stress/prominence.' Cites Sutton-Spence & Woll 1999 for BSL only in a list of grammatical descriptions; nothing on BSL word stress.

sources.citation: Fenlon, Jordan, Kearsy Cormier & Diane Brentari. 2017. The phonology of sign languages. In S. J. Hannahs & A. Bosch (eds.), The Routledge Handbook of Phonological Theory. London: Routledge. doi:10.4324/9781315675428-16. [UCL Discovery accepted manuscript, 34 pp.]
sources.note: Description explicitly centred on ASL and BSL. Treats the sign syllable as a sequential movement (Brentari 1998 syllable-counting criteria), notes the strong tendency to monosyllabic signs (83% of Stokoe et al. 1965 entries are single-movement) and that meaningful modifications are layered simultaneously rather than adding syllables. The only prominence remark is second-hand and about ASL phrasing (Wilbur & Zelaznik 1997: 'duration marks final phrase position and.. velocity marks prominence'). No statement of where stress/prominence falls within a BSL sign or prosodic word.
sources.venue: The Routledge Handbook of Phonological Theory
